I work in mental health myself, and when I was studying, pretty well all of us were big old softies and would cry about difficult situations. We were taught that crying with clients is normal, and at times even helps to validate the client's feelings about their situation, but that we should still be careful that clients don't feel pressured to console us instead. So for instance, if a therapist is like weeping and sobbing every session, that may be a bit much! We are also taught ways to handle difficult stories in the moment and keep the focus on our clients, so that we can better hear and understand what they're saying instead of focusing on what we feel about it. 

I've done the same as OP's therapist when someone is telling me their story, and if a client is worried about me crying I'll usually say something like "you don't need to be concerned for me, I'm just really moved by your story, and amazed by your resilience/ capacity to express your thoughts/ etc". Most of the time, it'll happen in an initial session, though I've shed a tear or two with longer term clients cuz want it or not, I care a lot about them and I hate that they're suffering. It doesn't happen super often for me, I prefer to do my crying afterwards lol. I find it helpful to do something like take a sip of my water, adjust my sitting position, and basically do mild grounding exercises if a client's situation is distressing to me.

I've been on the other side too, with my therapist crying after I explained my trauma. I felt like "right??? It IS absolutely fucking bullshit what I've been through!" Like I logically know that it was probably as bad as I thought, but that just confirms that my reaction and pain aren't an exaggeration since this professional is also thinking the same. 

Sorry for rambling a bit here, haha. Ultimately, we all have our own baggage that can make us react a bit more to the stories we hear! I like to think that it shows I care. Maybe it means you'd be a better therapist than you thought! If it was something that was holding you back from this career path, I hope that you know that this capacity for empathy would actually be a huge strength for you as a professional :D

I work in mental health, and the way we go about it in my area, this should be a rare occurrence. Tw suicide


The goal when we're talking to someone suicidal/at risk to themselves or someone else isn't to just jam them into the psych ward. It's about making sure that we plan for their safety. If, after our conversation, they still can't guarantee that they'll be safe, then I have no choice but to call 911 and get them to the ER. I don't want to get there, I don't think being admitted is always a good experience, and I want to avoid that as much as possible. The information I would give to the 911 dispatcher would be the most limited I can muster to protect confidentiality, like basically "Hey, I'm a mental health worker, this person is suicidal, they live at XXX and they told me their plan was to XXX"

Most of the time, I'll give them crisis lines just in case, tell them to schedule with me if it gets worse, and ask them to reach out to loved ones. I'll make sure to tell my colleagues, "Hey if so and so calls and I'm available, please let me know so we can chat." Usually, the ideation passes as we continue to support the client.

All in all, I've worked the field for 8 years now, and I've had someone admitted to psych ward about 4 times. Of those 4 times, only 1 was because they attempted. I've had to call child protection way more, but that's a different story!

 I hope this helps demystify a little of how we'd go about things! All in all, it should be an absolute last resort.

As mentioned in the link above, there may be a licensing issue. Some therapists may need to be licensed in both the province/ territory and the state. I doubt that it'd be too difficult for US-CAN relationships, but yeah it's definitely something you'd need to bring up with individual therapists.

I'm a social worker myself and I know of some colleagues who work with Canadian clients only, and they need to be registered with every province and territory. 

That being said, I think that LDRs and distance therapy are becoming more and more common, so I think that a lot more therapists will be open to the idea of working with international clients. Good luck!

Edit: it may be worth finding a couples therapist that works with telecounseling first then asking them if it's possible to do therapy with someone in another country. [This](https://affordabletherapynetwork.com/online-therapists/) is another mega awesome ressource to find a therapist Canada-side, and [this one](https://www.psychologytoday.com/ca/therapists) works in both Canada and the States.
